subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before an enquiry is made.
summary: Boca Med Spa is clearer than most about what it actually is. The copy says “We specialize in Medical Aesthetics”, the navigation names real categories — Skin, Body, Injectables, Laser Hair Removal, Infrared Skin Tightening — and the location is stated in the first sentence. A visitor who arrives knowing what they want can find it.

The difficulty is that the page gives them nowhere to go. The largest heading on the homepage is the word “Home”. There is no button, no booking link and no phone number anywhere on the first screen, on either desktop or mobile. The main message — “Total Skin and Body Transformation” — is baked into a picture rather than written as text, so it is soft at full width and invisible to search engines.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on desktop and mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. A score in this band points to structural gaps rather than cosmetic ones — and says nothing about the standard of treatment delivered in the room.

scorecard.finding: The largest heading on the page is the word “Home”.
No practitioner named, no credentials, no reviews on the homepage.
No call to action on the first screen; enquiry is by phone only.
Nothing on the first screen tells a visitor what to do next.
The hero message is an image that does not scale, and there is no tap-to-call.
Address and phone are present and consistent; location stated early.

strengthsLead: These are real advantages, and several of the recommendations below are about making them findable rather than building anything new.

strengths.title: The positioning is medical, not spa.
strengths.body: “We specialize in Medical Aesthetics” is stated plainly. A great many medspa sites blur this to sound more relaxing, and lose the patient who is making a clinical decision. This one does not.

strengths.title: The navigation names real categories.
strengths.body: Skin · Body · Waxing · Injectables · Laser Hair Removal · Infrared Skin Tightening · Matrix IR Wrinkle Reduction. A visitor with a specific concern can see where to go, which is more than many far newer sites manage.

strengths.title: The location appears in the first sentence.
strengths.body: “located in Boca Raton, FL” is exactly what someone searching locally needs to see immediately, and it is there.

strengths.title: Contact details are consistent.
strengths.body: The address at 600 S. Dixie Hwy and the number 561-447-2240 match across the site, which is more often wrong than right and matters for local search.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The page heading reads “Home”. There is no button, no booking link and no phone number on the first screen — the most prominent control is the search box.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. Same heading, and the banner image is reduced to a strip. Nothing on this screen can be tapped to make contact.

findings.heading: The largest heading on the homepage is the word “Home”.
findings.evidence: On both desktop and mobile, the page's main heading renders as “Home”, with the description beneath it. The practice name, the specialism and the location all appear in smaller supporting text.
findings.why: That heading is the first thing a screen reader announces and one of the strongest signals a search engine reads for the page. Spent on the word “Home”, it says nothing about medical aesthetics in Boca Raton — the two things a searching patient and Google both need.
findings.recommended: Replace it with what the practice actually is and where — the sort of line a patient could repeat to a friend. This is usually a single field in the page settings rather than a redesign.

findings.heading: There is nothing to click on the first screen.
findings.evidence: At 1366×768 the first screen shows the logo, navigation, social icons, a search box, the “Home” heading and the top of a banner image. No booking button, no enquiry link and no phone number appear. On mobile the same is true.
findings.why: A visitor who has decided in the first few seconds — which is when most decide — has nowhere to act. The most prominent interactive element on the page is the search box, which asks the patient to do the work of finding what they came for.
findings.recommended: One primary button on the first screen: “Book a Consultation”, with the phone number beside it as a tap-to-call link on mobile. This is the single highest-value change on this list.

findings.heading: No practitioner is named, and no reviews appear on the homepage.
findings.evidence: The homepage states “Our staff is extensively trained in Skin Care…”. No practitioner is named, no qualification, licence or supervising physician is given, and no patient review or rating appears anywhere on the page.
findings.why: For injectables and laser work the decisive question is who performs the treatment and what they are qualified to do. “Extensively trained” is a claim with no name behind it. A patient who cannot answer that question on the site usually answers it by choosing a practice where they can.
findings.recommended: Name the treating practitioner with their qualification and a real photograph, and place two or three patient reviews on the homepage near the point where someone would decide to enquire.

findings.heading: The main message is a picture of words, not words.
findings.evidence: “Total Skin and Body Transformation / NON-SURGICAL TREATMENTS / For Men & Woman” is part of the banner image rather than text on the page. At desktop width the lettering is visibly soft, and the line “For Men & Woman” contains a typing error that is fixed in the image file rather than in the page.
findings.why: Text inside an image cannot be read by search engines, cannot be enlarged by a patient who needs larger type, and goes soft whenever the image is stretched. It also means a small wording change requires a graphic designer instead of thirty seconds in the page editor.
findings.recommended: Set that message as real text over the photograph. The typo corrects itself in the process, and the line becomes searchable and sharp at every screen size.

findings.heading: Every enquiry has to become a phone call.
findings.evidence: No online booking or enquiry form was found from the homepage. The route to an appointment is the telephone number 561-447-2240.
findings.why: A large share of aesthetic research happens in the evening, when nobody is answering. Phone-only means the practice competes only during office hours, against clinics that accept a booking at eleven at night without anyone present.
findings.recommended: Add a booking path that completes on your own site. Even a short enquiry form with name, treatment of interest and preferred time captures the patient who will not phone a stranger.

findings.heading: On a phone, the banner becomes a strip and the message is unreadable.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 the banner image is scaled down to a narrow band, and the wording baked into it becomes small and indistinct. Below it the body copy is centred and set entirely in bold, which is harder to read at length than ordinary weight.
findings.why: Most aesthetic browsing is on a phone. The message the practice chose as its headline is the one thing a mobile visitor cannot comfortably read.
findings.recommended: Real text instead of image text solves this automatically, and the paragraph beneath reads better in regular weight, left-aligned.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Clinic sites conventionally lead with a booking button. This one leads with a search box, which places the effort on the patient.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: There is no action on the first mobile screen to reach — the nearest is a hamburger menu.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No review, rating or patient wording appears anywhere on the homepage.
“Our staff is extensively trained” — no name, no qualification, no photograph.
There is no next step offered on the first screen at all.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: Navigation is organised by concern rather than by machine name, which genuinely helps someone who does not know the treatment's brand.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “Total Skin and Body Transformation” is a large promise. Notes on suitability, downtime or who a treatment is not for would make the rest more credible.

roadmap.actions: Replace the “Home” heading with the practice, specialism and location. Add one primary booking button and a tap-to-call number to the first screen. Set the banner message as real text and correct “For Men & Woman”.
Name the treating practitioner with qualification and photograph. Add patient reviews to the homepage near the enquiry point. Add an enquiry form so contact does not depend on a phone call.

Practitioner and treatment authority content. Consistent listings across directories. Post-treatment review requests. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking, so the figures in the calculator above become yours rather than illustrative.

limitations: Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available).
